title: AI Vendor Evaluation
shortDefinition: A framework for assessing AI development vendors on technical depth, pricing transparency, IP ownership, and post-launch support.
definition: Evaluating an AI development vendor means assessing their technical depth on your specific use case, pricing transparency, IP and data ownership terms, validation/testing rigor, and post-launch support commitments — not just their portfolio or sales pitch. Many AI vendors look similar on the surface; the substantive differences usually show up in how they handle pricing transparency, technical documentation, and what happens after initial deployment.

sections.title: Key evaluation criteria beyond the sales pitch
sections.description: Look for pricing transparency, IP ownership clarity, validation methodology, and post-launch support.

content.text: Look for: transparent, specific pricing rather than 'contact us for a custom quote' with no published ranges; clear answers about who owns the resulting IP and model; explicit discussion of validation methodology (how will you know the model actually works, not just that it was delivered); documented post-launch support and what happens if the model needs adjustment after real-world deployment; and willingness to discuss what they *can't* do well, not just an unbounded yes to every request. Vendors confident in their work are typically comfortable being specific and transparent on all of these dimensions.

items: Transparent pricing — specific ranges, not just 'contact us.'
IP ownership clarity — who owns the resulting model and code.
Validation methodology — how will success be measured?
Post-launch support — what happens after deployment?
Honest scope — willingness to discuss what they can't do well.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Vendors confident in their work are comfortable being specific and transparent on pricing, IP, validation, and support.

Be cautious of vendors who won't provide any pricing indication before a lengthy sales process, who claim a single AI approach (usually 'just use the latest LLM') solves every problem regardless of fit, who don't discuss validation or testing methodology at all, who are vague about data handling and IP ownership terms, or who promise unrealistic timelines for genuinely complex projects. These patterns often indicate either inexperience with the realistic complexity of production AI systems, or a sales-first approach prioritizing closing the deal over setting realistic expectations.

items: No upfront pricing — lengthy sales process before any indication.
One-size-fits-all — claims one approach solves every problem.
No validation discussion — doesn't discuss how success is measured.
Vague terms — unclear on data handling and IP ownership.
Unrealistic timelines — promises that don't match project complexity.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of vendor evaluation

content.text: Vendor evaluation has limitations. Even thorough evaluation can't guarantee project success — vendor capabilities in practice depend on team quality and project management. Past work examples may not reflect current team depth, and sales promises may not match delivery. References from vendors are often curated, and pricing transparency varies significantly across the industry. Evaluation also doesn't account for vendor stability or long-term viability, which can affect ongoing support and maintenance.

items: Evaluation limits — can't guarantee project success.
Team quality — past work may not reflect current team.
Sales vs. delivery — promises may not match execution.
Curated references — vendors show their best work.
Pricing opacity — varies significantly across the industry.
Vendor stability — evaluation doesn't account for long-term viability.

content.title: Important
content.text: Vendor evaluation is essential but not foolproof. Combine evaluation criteria with references, small proof-of-concept work, and clear contractual terms.

sections.title: Best practices for AI vendor evaluation

content.text: Evaluating AI vendors effectively requires systematic criteria, references, and validation. The following practices can help ensure you choose a vendor that delivers genuine value.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Define clear evaluation criteria before starting vendor conversations.
Ask for pricing ranges upfront — published ranges are a positive signal.
Get specific answers on IP ownership, data handling, and validation.
Ask about limitations — what types of projects are not a good fit?
Request references and follow up on specific project outcomes.
Consider a small proof-of-concept before committing to full project.
Review contracts carefully — especially IP, data, and support terms.
Trust patterns of transparency and specificity over polished sales materials.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Evaluate transparency and specificity — vendors who give clear, specific answers across pricing, IP, and validation are more likely to deliver than those who are vague.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about AI vendor evaluation

items.question: Why won't some AI vendors give any pricing information upfront?
items.answer: Some vendors prefer a lengthy sales process before discussing pricing, which can indicate either highly variable project scoping needs or a sales approach prioritizing engagement over transparency; ClickMasters publishes specific pricing ranges by project type instead.

items.question: What questions should I ask an AI vendor before signing a contract?
items.answer: Ask about validation methodology (how will success be measured), IP and data ownership terms, post-launch support scope, realistic timeline given your project's actual complexity, and specific pricing for your use case type.

items.question: Should I be skeptical of a vendor promising very fast timelines for a complex AI project?
items.answer: Genuinely complex AI projects (custom models, multi-system integrations, regulated industries) typically require meaningful validation time; unrealistically fast promises can indicate corners being cut on testing and validation.

items.question: How important is published pricing transparency when evaluating vendors?
items.answer: It's a meaningful signal of how the vendor operates more broadly — published, specific pricing suggests confidence and standardized processes, though it's one factor among several worth evaluating.

items.question: What's the difference between a vendor that builds a working demo and one that builds a production system?
items.answer: A production system requires validation, monitoring, error handling, and support infrastructure well beyond what a demo needs to show — ask specifically about this distinction when evaluating vendor proposals.

items.question: Where can I see ClickMasters' specific pricing for my use case?
items.answer: See our full pricing guide for detailed ranges by project type and industry, or book a free consultation for a specific quote.

items.question: What is IP ownership in AI development and why does it matter?
items.answer: IP ownership determines who owns the model, code, and data generated during the project. Clear terms are essential — without them, you may not own the AI model you paid to build. ClickMasters ensures full IP transfer on all projects.

items.question: What is validation methodology in AI project evaluation?
items.answer: Validation methodology is how the vendor will measure whether the model actually works — test data, performance metrics, and acceptance criteria. Vendors should specify this before the project starts, not after.

items.question: How do I assess a vendor's technical depth on my specific use case?
items.answer: Ask for examples of similar projects, discuss their approach to your specific data type and problem, and ask about potential challenges specific to your domain. A confident vendor will have direct, specific answers.

items.question: What are the tradeoffs between niche AI specialists and generalist AI development companies?
items.answer: Specialists often have deeper domain expertise and proven patterns but may be limited in scope. Generalists offer broader capabilities but may lack domain depth. The right choice depends on your specific needs and project complexity.
